Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh” A **hillshade** layer is just a *paint* layer that turns the raw elevation values from a `raster-dem` source into a black-and-white relief image. If the result looks like: * very dark shadows / very bright highlights * “chalky” ridges that drown out the underlying map * a flat-looking surface when you tilt the map the problem is almost always one (or a combination) of these: | What it is | Typical cause | |------------|----------------| | **Too much contrast** | Default `hillshade-exaggeration` (0.5) + default `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` (pure black / pure white). | | **Single-direction lighting** | `hillshade-method` left at its default **`standard`** – the light comes from one direction, so shadows are deep and highlights are crisp. | | **No alpha on the light colors** | Black/white with `opacity: 1` makes the shadows/highlights completely opaque, covering any imagery underneath. | | **Stacked hillshade layers** | Adding several hillshade layers with different illumination directions was the old “multidirectional” hack. It forces the renderer to draw the DEM many times, which is expensive and still produces harsh edges. | | **Wrong illumination anchor** | `hillshade-illumination-anchor: "viewport"` keeps the light fixed to the screen; when you rotate the map the light no longer matches the terrain orientation, making the shading feel “off”. | --- ## The Modern, One-Layer Fix (MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.5) MapLibre 5.5 introduced the **`hillshade-method`** paint property. With a single hillshade layer you can get a soft, natural-looking relief without any extra draw passes. ### 1. Use `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` ```json { "id": "hillshade", "type": "hillshade", "source": "terrain-dem", // your raster-dem source "paint": { // 1️⃣ Soft, multi-directional lighting in ONE pass "hillshade-method": "multidirectional", // 2️⃣ Reduce overall contrast (default is 0.5) "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4, // 3️⃣ Make the light follow the map rotation (optional but usually nicer) "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", // 4️⃣ Warm, semi-transparent shadows "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30, 40, 80, 0.45)", // 5️⃣ Light, semi-transparent highlights "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255, 240, 200, 0.4)" } } ``` **What each line does** | Property | Effect | |----------|--------| | `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` | Lights the terrain from several directions in a single shader pass. This alone softens the harsh black-and-white look dramatically. | | `hillshade-exaggeration` | Scales the intensity of the shading. Lower values → gentler relief. | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | `"map"` makes the light rotate with the map (so north-facing slopes stay lit when you spin the map). Keep `"viewport"` only if you want a fixed “sun-over-the-top-of-the-screen” effect. | | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Use **rgba** with an alpha < 1 so the underlying imagery can still be seen. Choose cool shadows and warm highlights for a more natural look. | ### 2. Remove any extra hillshade layers If you previously tried to “soften” the result by adding a second hillshade layer with a different illumination direction, **delete it**. The `multidirectional` method replaces that hack and is far cheaper (only one draw pass). ```js // ❌ Bad – old way (remove) map.addLayer({ id: "hillshade-extra", type: "hillshade", source: "terrain-dem", paint: { "hillshade-illumination-direction": 45 } }); ``` ### 3. (Optional) Tweak the contrast further If you still need a little more or less contrast after the above, adjust **one** of the following: ```json // Make shadows a bit darker (more contrast) "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(20,30,60,0.55)" // Or make them lighter (less contrast) "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(40,55,90,0.35)" // Same for highlights "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,250,230,0.3)" ``` ### 4. Verify the version `hillshade-method` was added in **MapLibre GL JS 5.5**. If you are on an older version the property will be ignored and you’ll still see the harsh default. Upgrade: ```html ``` --- ## Full Minimal Example ```html Soft Hillshade
``` *The hillshade now looks gentle, the underlying map is still visible, and you only pay the cost of **one** DEM draw pass.* --- ## Quick Checklist (copy-paste into your own notes) - [ ] **One** `hillshade` layer, `type: "hillshade"`. - [ ] `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` (GL JS ≥ 5.5). - [ ] Reduce `hillshade-exaggeration` (e.g., `0.4`). - [ ] Use `rgba(..., α)` for `hillshade-shadow-color` and `hillshade-highlight-color` (α ≈ 0.4-0.5). - [ ] Set `hillshade-illumination-anchor: "map"` (optional but usually better). - [ ] Remove any extra hillshade layers that were added for “multiple directions”. - [ ] Verify you are running MapLibre GL JS 5.5 or newer. Follow those steps and the harsh, black-and-white hillshade will become a smooth, natural-looking relief that plays nicely with any basemap underneath. Happy mapping!
